concept.name: ARMA model
concept.definition: A time-series model combining an autoregressive part of order p and a moving-average part of order q, expressing a stationary series as a function of its own lagged values and lagged innovations. Box and Jenkins popularized a systematic identification-estimation-validation methodology for ARMA models.
concept.intuition: ARMA captures both ways the past echoes into the present: through the series' own lagged levels and through lingering shocks.
concept.mechanics: ARMA(p,q): X_t = delta + phi_1*X_{t-1} + ... + phi_p*X_{t-p} + A_t - theta_1*A_{t-1} - ... - theta_q*A_{t-q}. By the Wold decomposition any weakly stationary process can be approximated by an ARMA model. Fitting requires a stationary series (difference first if needed, giving ARIMA), moderately long samples (roughly 50-100+ observations), and maximum likelihood estimation; ACF/PACF patterns guide the choice of p and q.
concept.formula: X_t = delta + sum_{i=1..p} phi_i*X_{t-i} + A_t - sum_{j=1..q} theta_j*A_{t-j}, with A_t white noise.
concept.failure_modes: ARMA assumes linearity, stationarity, and time-invariant parameters; structural breaks, regime changes, and volatility clustering in financial data violate these, so fitted models deteriorate out of sample. Parameter redundancy (near-common AR/MA factors) causes identification problems.
concept.misconceptions: That a high in-sample ARMA fit implies the series is predictable going forward; in-sample fit does not establish out-of-sample forecast skill, and near-zero-return predictability in asset prices is the empirical norm.
concept.example: An ARMA(1,1) fitted to a stationary macro series uses last period's value and last period's shock to forecast, identified by decaying patterns in both the ACF and PACF.

citations.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Section 6.4.4.5 Box-Jenkins Models
